key_insight: The paper reframes AI development through a strong sustainability lens: natural capital is non‑substitutable, so AI growth must be bounded by biophysical limits and designed to operate within planetary boundaries.
problem_solved: Addresses the unchecked environmental and material impacts of expanding AI (compute, energy, raw materials) and the prevailing 'weak sustainability' assumption that technology can substitute for degraded natural systems; provides a framework to align AI development with ecological limits and governance needs.
method: Articulate strong‑sustainability principles specific to AI (non‑substitutability of natural capital; absolute caps on resource/energy use; lifecycle thinking).
Develop measurable metrics and limits (compute/energy budgets, embodied material footprints, alignment with planetary boundaries) and recommend lifecycle assessment (LCA) approaches.
Propose policy and design interventions (efficiency standards, procurement rules, training/operational energy caps, reuse/recycling incentives, transparency and governance mechanisms).
impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners concrete criteria and interventions to measure and reduce ecological impacts, prioritize efficient model design and reuse, and engage with policy levers to keep AI development within planetary limits.
visual_elements: Side‑by‑side diagram: 'Weak vs Strong Sustainability' showing substitutability vs non‑substitutability of natural capital.
Sankey or lifecycle flowchart of an AI model showing embedded materials, manufacturing, training energy, inference energy and hotspots.
Bar/line chart comparing energy/CO2 footprints of model classes with an overlaid 'biophysical budget' cap.
Policy/roadmap icon set: metrics → standards → procurement → governance (timeline or checklist).
paper_title: A strong sustainability approach to AI development
